title: India and China Are Talking Again — Quietly, Carefully, and With 100,000 Troops Still on the Border
excerpt: NSA Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met in New Delhi last week and used the word both sides had been avoiding for years: 'normalisation.' But the LAC is still bristling with soldiers.
body:
For five years, India and China managed their relationship the way neighbours manage a property dispute — through lawyers, go-betweens, and a studied refusal to make eye contact. Last week, they sat down at the same table in New Delhi and used the word both capitals had been carefully avoiding: normalisation.

National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met on the sidelines of the 16th BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting, which India hosted as this year's BRICS chair. The Ministry of External Affairs described the exchange as "constructive and forward-looking" — bureaucratic code, but a significant upgrade from the frosty communiqués of years past. Both sides "noted progress towards gradual normalisation," the statement said.

In his remarks, Doval signalled that Prime Minister Narendra Modi would shortly visit China for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, expected in late August in Tianjin. It would be Modi's first visit to China in years and a diplomatic milestone that would have been unthinkable as recently as 2023.

## The Long Shadow of Galwan


![Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg)



> **""NSA Doval underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building of trust and better understanding," the MEA's spokesman said."**



The backdrop to any India-China conversation remains the Galwan Valley clash of June 2020, when hand-to-hand combat along the Line of Actual Control killed 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese troops — the first deadly border engagement between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in 45 years.

What followed was a military mobilisation that neither side has fully reversed. Each country maintains between 50,000 and 60,000 troops along the LAC in eastern Ladakh. While disengagement from the most contested friction points was completed in late 2024, de-escalation — the pullback of frontline forces and heavy equipment — has not happened. The border, in other words, is quiet. It is not relaxed.

India's foreign ministry has been cautious not to oversell the thaw. "NSA Doval underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building of trust and better understanding," the MEA's spokesman said. The emphasis on *stability* over *friendship* is deliberate. New Delhi wants a relationship it can predict, not necessarily one it celebrates.

## Parallel Tracks


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


Wang Yi, for his part, urged "the resumption of bilateral dialogue mechanisms" and called for expanded exchanges in trade, finance, law enforcement, and media. Beijing has also pushed for BRICS to "hold high the banner of multilateralism" — a pointed reference to Western-led structures that China increasingly frames as exclusionary.

The diplomacy is running on two parallel tracks. The BRICS NSA meeting gave both sides a multilateral pretext to hold bilateral talks without the optics of a standalone China outreach. At the same time, China's ambassador to India has been unusually active on social media, congratulating India on its BRICS hosting and signalling openness.

But the structural tensions remain formidable. India's participation in the US-led Quad, its growing defence partnership with Washington, its role in supply-chain diversification away from China, and the recent Pax Silica AI governance summit — all sit uncomfortably beside the normalisation narrative. For Beijing, India's deepening ties with the US represent a strategic hedge that limits how far rapprochement can go.

## The Diaspora Calculus

For the Indian diaspora, the India-China dynamic is not abstract geopolitics. It shapes the semiconductor supply chains that employ thousands of Indian engineers in Silicon Valley. It determines whether Indian startups can access Chinese venture capital — a pipeline that has essentially frozen since 2020. And it underpins the strategic calculus of defence spending, border infrastructure, and the broader question of whether India can position itself as the alternative to China for global manufacturing.

The Doval-Wang meeting was not a breakthrough. It was something potentially more useful: a mechanism. India and China are building the plumbing of a relationship that can function without warmth — one that can handle crises without collapsing and manage disagreements without escalation. The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra has resumed. Tourist visas for Chinese nationals have been restored. Trade, despite the tensions, crossed $135 billion last year.

Whether that plumbing can hold when the next pressure point arrives — Taiwan, a LAC incident, a trade dispute — is the question neither Doval nor Wang answered last week. They did not need to. For now, the fact that they were in the same room, using the same word, was enough.
